A.explanation: Gravitational potential energy depends on weight times vertical change of the centre of mass, not on the $force$ versus $extension$ area for stretching.

B.explanation: The graph goes beyond the straight elastic part to plastic behaviour, so unloading would follow a different path and return less energy than was put in.

C.explanation: Some work beyond the elastic limit ends as heat and permanent deformation, but the whole area includes stored elastic energy as well as that part.

D.explanation: For a stretching force, small work $F \Delta x$ summed over the extension equals the area under the $force$-$extension$ graph.

hints: Look at the axes of the diagram: vertical $force$ in $\text{N}$ against horizontal $extension$ in $\text{m}$, with an initial straight part then a curved plastic part.
Recall that stretching work is built up from $work = force \times extension$ for small steps, so $\text{N} \times \text{m} = \text{J}$ suggests an area meaning.
Ask whether all that input energy would come back if the final load were removed, given the curve has passed the elastic limit into permanent extension.
walkthrough: Identify what is plotted: the stretching $force$ on the y-axis and the resulting $extension$ from $0$ on the x-axis, first linear then curving over as the wire yields.
State the governing rule: work done by a varying force is the sum of $F \Delta x$ for each small increase in extension, which is the area between the curve and the extension axis.
Apply it to the whole loading: adding up every strip under the complete curve from $0$ to the final extension gives the total energy transferred to the wire during stretching.

Check the distractors: recoverable energy on unloading would be only the area under the unloading line, and heat from plastic flow is only part of the total, while gravitational potential energy of the wire is unrelated.
Therefore the area under the whole loading graph is the total work done in stretching the wire. This is option D
